text: Given an array sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates in place so each unique element appears once, keeping the order, and return the count k. The first k elements must hold the unique values; the rest can be anything.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Since the array is sorted, duplicates are always next to each other. I change the array in place with constant extra space, and I return the length — the judge only checks the first k. So I don't even need to clean up the tail. Is that right?

Okay. So really I'm building a prefix of unique values at the front of the same array. One index marks where the next unique value goes, and a scan reads through everything. That index only moves when I keep something, and at the end it equals k.

Let me think about the options. A hash set of seen values works, but it costs linear extra space. Erasing duplicates one by one is quadratic, because every erase shifts the rest. This problem reminds me of the fast-slow two-pointer pattern, used as a write pointer: the fast pointer decides what to read, the slow one decides what to keep and where to write it. Since the array is sorted, a value is a duplicate exactly when it equals the last kept value, nums of i minus one. That gives linear time and constant space.

Here's the plan. One: start the write index i at zero. Two: for each number, skip it if i is above zero and it equals nums of i minus one. Three: otherwise write it at i, move i forward, and finally return i. Two things worth flagging. The i above zero guard avoids reading index minus one on the first element, which is always kept. And the overwrite is safe: i never passes the scan position, so I only overwrite cells I've already read. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop: i is the write index, and num walks through the array. If i is above zero and num equals nums of i minus one, I continue; otherwise I write nums of i plus plus equals num. Then I return i. One thing worth flagging — I compare against nums of i minus one, the last kept value, not the previous element of the scan. Here both happen to work, but the last-kept version is the one that stays correct when I change the rule, say to keep two copies.

Let's dry-run the code on zero, zero, one, one, two — expected three. The row that matters is where the first one shows up: it doesn't equal the last kept zero, so it's written at index one, on top of the duplicate zero I skipped. That's the safe overwrite in action. The two then lands at index two, and i ends at three, with zero, one, two up front. That matches. Corner cases: a single element gives one; all identical gives one; all unique gives n.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass, constant work per element. Space is constant — a single write index, in place. One more thing — the same skeleton solves a whole family by swapping the keep rule: compare against nums of i minus two to allow two copies, keep values not equal to a target to remove that value, or keep only non-zero values when moving zeroes. Same write pointer, different condition.
Nicely done. Three things stood out: the write-pointer framing, comparing against the last kept value using the sorted property, and generalizing the keep rule to the whole family. Good work.
